data.turoyo: kəmmo af fərṭaʕnayḏan ġalabe ne, ksulqono l qarʕe du quṣro d nəfṣono ǧuli
data.translation: Sie sagt: Wir haben viele Flöhe, ich steige auf die Zinnen des Schlosses, um meine Kleider auszuschütteln.

rationale: New Infectum box: explicit purpose and first-person feminine speaker shaking clothes.

data.turoyo: Hiye qayəm mi gurto, nfəṣle ruḥe, ela zbiṭole qum ṣadre w naḥət bi kaše.
data.translation: Er stand auf aus der Grube, schob sich an sie heran, packte sie vor sich und eilte den Abhang hinunter.

rationale: Thin Preterit: reflexive ruḥe argument with physical self-motion; not evidence for a distinct forward-direction sense.

summary: The new Infectum purpose form nəfṣono preserves the source's female speaker and absence of ko-. Active Preterit uses -L agent morphology; ruḥe can be its reflexive object without Detransitive morphology.

The separate npṣ entry has the same core gloss and an existing npəṣle ruḥe 'schüttelte sich' quotation. This argues against automatically lexicalizing the German forward-motion reading at 70/143. No other entry is changed.

The sword token mfəṣle is retained only as a provisional occurrence index. Lookup finds no attested nfṣ form with that exact spelling; assimilation is plausible but not proven. The nearby tailoring root fṣl does not fit the clause's sword-and-strike sequence.
No idiom is added: self-directed shaking/pushing is compositional on this evidence. Existing bed and fur-cloak examples are not duplicated.
At 70/143 does nfəṣle ruḥe mean shake oneself/free or propel oneself? The supplied German gives an approach to the woman, but the Turoyo has no overt goal phrase.
Verify mfəṣle at PrS 19/66 in the edition: nasal assimilation from nfṣ, a transcription issue, or another lexical item? Does it mean draw, thrust or swing the sword?
Confirm the mapping of existing prs 43/23 to supplied PrS 18/30 before correcting the bed example citation.
Do editors want nfṣ and npṣ linked as variants? Their consonant-specific entries are retained here.
